# Original ViT Against CNN Backbones: A Backbone-Role Review

## Abstract

The original ViT and CNN backbones differ mainly in backbone interface and data dependence, not just accuracy. Plain ViT embeds fixed image patches and applies global self-attention; its strongest early classification results required large-scale pretraining such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M. ResNet-like CNNs use local shared kernels and expose progressively downsampled, multi-stage maps suited to established detection and segmentation heads. Full attention also costs quadratically more as token count rises. Dense-prediction evidence mostly concerns modified Transformers: RetinaNet with PVT-Small reached 40.4 AP on COCO val2017 versus 36.3 AP with ResNet-50, but PVT adds a pyramid and spatial-reduction attention, so this is not a plain-ViT result. Modern benchmarks likewise mix architectures and pretraining; Battle of the Backbones reports supervised CNNs strongest on most considered tasks and greater ViT sensitivity to data and scale. ViTs and CNNs are not interchangeable feature extractors even at similar accuracy. CKA analyses find more uniform, grid-like representations across ViT layers, clearer stage separation in ResNets, and link the ViT pattern to early global aggregation and strong residual propagation. Behavioral comparisons also show that similar ImageNet accuracy and compute can coexist with different mistakes, calibration, transferability, and invariances. Thus, no universal winner is supported. Plain ViT is a strong global classifier in large-data regimes, while CNNs provide mature hierarchical maps and a broad-task baseline. Pyramid, hybrid, or adapted Transformers may improve dense prediction or efficiency, but only under their specific architectures, pretraining, heads, datasets, and hardware conditions. ## Introduction

This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with convolutional neural-network backbones, using the organizing choice of backbone role rather than treating every later hybrid as a new version of ViT. The central question is not simply whether attention can replace convolution in classification: it is how a patch-based, globally attentive feature extractor compares with CNN feature extractors when both are used as backbones for recognition and downstream vision systems. CNN backbones such as ResNets and ResNeXts became the standard reusable feature extractors after large-scale ImageNet training, using local shared kernels whose receptive fields grow with depth and whose hierarchical feature maps fit detectors and segmenters. ViT instead entered vision as a convolution-free sequence model that splits an image into fixed patch tokens and applies standard Transformer self-attention across them; later work emphasizes that this plain design is distinct from vision-specific hierarchical Transformers and adapted CNN–Transformer backbones. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:12bdfdbebcf4] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63]

The scope therefore separates three levels of evidence. First, the original ViT should be understood as a classification-oriented, single-scale token backbone whose strongest early results depended on large-scale pretraining. Second, conventional CNN backbones should be assessed as hierarchical, locally connected feature extractors that were already integrated into dense-prediction pipelines. Third, later models such as PVT, CvT, LeViT, HVT, ConTNet, and ViT-CoMer respond to particular ViT limitations—resolution, hierarchy, local context, efficiency, optimization, or reuse of pretrained weights—but their results should not be read as direct measurements of the original ViT unless the training data, model size, task, decoder, and hardware conditions are matched. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:15bbb833ac5f] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:e4e92da5f487] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2103.14899:section:abstract:1:78640899c791:claim:efb5e17d94e6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

The comparison also needs to distinguish architecture from pretraining and task objective. Battle of the Backbones reports that, across more than 1,500 runs spanning classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and other tasks, supervised convolutional models remained strongest on most tasks among the backbones considered, while also finding that ViTs were more sensitive to pretraining-data amount and parameter count than CNNs. That benchmark concerns many modern backbones and training paradigms, so it contextualizes rather than directly ranks the original ViT against ResNet. Likewise, analyses beyond ImageNet accuracy show that ConvNets and ViTs with similar accuracy and compute can differ in errors, calibration, transferability, invariance, and internal representations. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:2af299151cfa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be] [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:641138c80176] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7935f0e4436d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f]

Accordingly, the remainder of this review is grouped by mechanism and evidence: classification criteria, the original ViT and CNN mechanisms, matched or partially matched experimental results, and concrete trade-offs. Dense-prediction evidence is especially important because a backbone must supply spatially localized, often multi-scale features, not only an image-level class prediction. For example, PVT was explicitly motivated by ViT's low-resolution outputs and high computational and memory cost for dense tasks; under a comparable parameter count, RetinaNet with PVT-Small reached 40.4 AP on COCO val2017 versus 36.3 AP with ResNet-50. That result demonstrates a later pyramid Transformer's downstream advantage in that setup, but it does not establish that the original, unmodified ViT would outperform ResNet-50 under the same detector and training conditions. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:12bdfdbebcf4]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the taxonomy is organized by backbone role: what spatial representation a feature extractor exposes, how tokens or feature maps change through depth, and whether the architecture can be inserted directly into classification and dense-prediction pipelines. This is a review grouping for comparing the original ViT with CNN backbones; it is not a universal taxonomy and should not be attributed as a fixed classification to the individual papers. Under that grouping, a conventional CNN backbone is typically hierarchical: local convolution kernels share weights over space, stages progressively downsample feature maps, and receptive fields enlarge as depth increases. The original ViT instead begins with fixed, usually non-overlapping image patches, embeds them as one token sequence, and applies global self-attention across that sequence rather than constructing a conventional CNN feature pyramid by default. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:12bdfdbebcf4] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63]

The first classification axis is output scale and spatial resolution. CNN backbones such as ResNet and ResNeXt provide stage-wise multi-scale feature maps that detectors and segmenters can consume through feature pyramids or decoder heads. The plain ViT paradigm is described as single-scale: it can exploit strong open-source ViT pretraining, but its limited scale diversity is insufficient for many dense-prediction requirements. Vision-specific pyramid Transformers such as PVT address this by redesigning the network into a progressive shrinking pyramid with spatial-reduction attention, whereas adapted backbones such as ViT-CoMer keep the plain ViT branch and add convolutional multi-scale features. These are distinct solutions to the same interface problem: a backbone used for detection or segmentation must provide localized, multi-resolution features, while an image classifier may only need a global representation. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:de8f23109ad5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:12bdfdbebcf4]

The second axis is locality versus global context. Convolution builds local receptive fields, translation-equivariant weight sharing, and spatial subsampling into its basic operation; stacked layers can eventually cover a large image region, but early layers do not attend globally in the ViT sense. ViT self-attention lets token positions interact dynamically over the full patch sequence, which representation analyses link to early aggregation of global information. CvT illustrates a hybrid position in this dimension: convolutional token embeddings and depth-wise-separable convolutional projections add overlapping local context, hierarchy, and subsampling while retaining Transformer attention. Thus, “CNN,” “plain ViT,” and “hybrid” should be separated by mechanism rather than treated as a simple accuracy label. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324]

The third axis is positional encoding and input-resolution behavior. Standard ViT patch tokens need positional information because self-attention itself is permutation invariant; the original design therefore adds positional embeddings to patch embeddings. CvT reports that its convolutional design can remove positional embedding without performance degradation, which it presents as simplifying transfer to higher-resolution vision tasks. HVT instead progressively pools tokens to shorten the sequence, explicitly analogizing token downsampling to CNN feature-map downsampling. These criteria matter because changing resolution, token length, or position handling can affect both compute and compatibility with downstream heads; they are not merely implementation details. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

The fourth axis is training dependence and optimization regime. Early ViT results showed that a pure Transformer could match or exceed strong CNNs in image classification when trained on sufficiently large data such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M; later work also notes that ViT-style models can be sensitive to learning rate, epochs, optimizer, augmentation, regularization, pretraining-data scale, and model size. CNN backbones established a different operating point as reusable, supervised ImageNet feature extractors, while later data-efficient and distilled Transformers reduced some of ViT's data requirements. Consequently, architecture family should not be conflated with pretraining recipe: a ViT trained on JFT, a CNN trained on ImageNet-1k, and a self-supervised backbone are not interchangeable observations even if their ImageNet top-1 scores are close. [E:arxiv:2103.14899:section:abstract:1:78640899c791:claim:efb5e17d94e6] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be]

The final axis separates task objective from efficiency objective. Classification asks for an image-level prediction; dense prediction asks for pixel-, box-, or mask-level outputs and therefore stresses resolution, localization, and multi-scale features. Efficiency-oriented designs form another related but different objective: LeViT reuses CNN principles such as decreasing activation-map resolutions and adds attention bias to optimize the speed–accuracy tradeoff for fast image classification, while HVT pools tokens to reduce sequence cost. Edge-splitting or model-pruning systems address deployment latency after a model exists and should not be confused with backbone taxonomy. Likewise, a formal unified view can interpret vision Transformers as CNNs with dynamic convolutions, but that analytical equivalence is a design-space perspective; it does not erase the practical differences in tokenization, feature hierarchy, pretraining, and downstream interfaces that govern the original ViT–CNN comparison. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:e4e92da5f487] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:905803bb481a] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:6f8729d848c1] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:9f0c90858395] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

## Representative Methods

The original ViT mechanism is deliberately close to a text Transformer: an image is divided into fixed-size, non-overlapping patches, each patch is linearly embedded, positional embeddings are added, and the resulting sequence is processed by repeated standard Transformer encoder blocks containing multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers. Its contribution was to show that a pure, convolution-free attention model could attain state-of-the-art image-classification performance against ResNets and EfficientNets when pretraining was large enough, specifically in regimes such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M. The applicability boundary is therefore central: the original architecture was primarily a global, single-scale image classifier rather than a ready-made feature pyramid for detectors and segmenters. Its evidence supports large-scale classification and transfer, not by itself a claim that the same token interface is efficient or optimal for high-resolution dense prediction. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b] Inside ViT, self-attention computes interactions among patch tokens rather than applying a fixed local kernel. This gives every token a path to information from the entire image at each attention layer, but the cost of full attention grows with the square of token count; high-resolution images therefore create substantially larger attention matrices and memory use. Representation analyses identify two consequences of this design. First, self-attention enables early aggregation of global information. Second, ViT residual connections strongly propagate lower-layer features into higher layers. These mechanisms help explain why ViT layers exhibit a more uniform representation structure than ResNet layers, but they do not imply that ViT automatically supplies the stage-wise spatial hierarchy used by common dense-prediction heads. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:bc8ff296c103] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7935f0e4436d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:c1fb2c740395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] The original ViT also preserves spatial information in token form: patch tokens retain a mapping back to locations on the input grid even though the model reasons over them as a sequence. The analysis by Raghu et al. finds that ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from the classification method used. This distinction matters for backbone comparison: ViT is not spatially blind, but its native representation is a sequence of equal-resolution patch tokens plus a class token, rather than the conventional stack of progressively downsampled CNN feature maps. Thus, localization potential and convenient multi-scale backbone output are different properties and should not be conflated. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:bc8ff296c103] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7935f0e4436d]

Conventional CNN backbones use a different inductive mechanism. A convolution kernel is applied locally with shared weights across spatial positions; stacked convolutional blocks expand the effective receptive field as network depth increases, while pooling or strided operations reduce spatial resolution and increase channel capacity. ResNet's skip connections made very deep convolutional networks practical, and ResNet/ResNeXt-style models became established reusable backbones because their stage outputs provide hierarchical feature maps for classification, detection, and segmentation. PVT's characterization of CNN backbones captures the key contrast: their local receptive fields increase with depth, whereas a Transformer can model global relations directly. The CNN contribution is therefore not merely convolution as an operator, but a mature hierarchy of local, translation-equivariant feature extraction with dense-prediction-compatible intermediate maps. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:12bdfdbebcf4] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] The CNN mechanism also builds in locality, weight sharing, and spatial subsampling. CvT describes these properties as encouraging local spatial structure and providing some degree of shift, scale, and distortion invariance, while hierarchical kernels learn patterns from low-level edges and textures to higher-level semantic patterns. These architectural priors can reduce the amount of data or optimization machinery needed to learn basic visual structure, which is relevant when comparing CNNs with ViT's more general sequence-processing architecture. However, the same local priors constrain a single convolutional layer's receptive field; long-range relations in a CNN must generally emerge through depth, larger kernels, dilation, attention modules, or other structural modifications. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] ResNet and similar CNNs are backbones in the operational sense: they expose multi-stage feature maps that can be connected to RetinaNet, Mask R-CNN, segmentation decoders, and other task-specific heads. This is why CNN backbones became common components across computer-vision systems rather than only standalone classifiers. Their applicability boundary is the reverse of plain ViT's: CNNs are naturally suited to local and hierarchical feature extraction, but ordinary convolutional layers do not perform ViT-style dynamic global token mixing at every block. A CNN can achieve a large aggregate receptive field, but that should not be described as identical to direct self-attention over all image patches. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:12bdfdbebcf4] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f]

The first major family of later responses is the pyramid Transformer. PVT retains a convolution-free Transformer backbone but changes the plain-ViT interface by constructing a progressive shrinking pyramid and using spatial-reduction attention. The pyramid learns multi-scale, high-resolution features while reducing the computation and memory burden of large feature maps; spatial-reduction attention shrinks the keys and values when processing high-resolution tokens. PVT's contribution was to make a pure Transformer usable as a drop-in backbone for representative dense-prediction pipelines such as RetinaNet and Mask R-CNN, and PVT plus DETR was presented as an entirely convolution-free detection pipeline. Its boundary is that it is a redesigned vision-specific backbone, not the original ViT model. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:15bbb833ac5f] PVT also clarifies the comparison with both sides of the original debate. Against CNNs, its designers argue that a global receptive field at each Transformer stage is more suitable for detection and segmentation than receptive fields that only become global after many convolutional layers. Against plain ViT, they argue that the pyramid structure and spatial-reduction attention solve low-resolution output, high compute, high memory use, and poor fit to dense-prediction pipelines. Therefore, PVT should be treated as evidence that Transformer backbones can be adapted to pixel-level tasks, not as evidence that the original single-scale ViT already had the same feature-map interface or efficiency profile. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:15bbb833ac5f]

CvT takes the hybrid route by inserting convolutional structure into ViT rather than building a convolution-free pyramid. Its convolutional token embedding uses overlapping strided convolutions on a two-dimensional token grid, capturing local context, reducing sequence length, and increasing feature dimension across stages. Its convolutional Transformer block replaces the linear attention projections with depth-wise separable convolutional projections, adding local spatial context and allowing strided key/value subsampling for efficiency. The claimed mechanism is a combination of CNN properties—local receptive fields, shared weights, and spatial subsampling—with Transformer properties—dynamic attention, global context fusion, and generalization. CvT's applicability is as a hierarchical hybrid classifier and transfer model; it is neither a plain ViT nor a conventional all-convolutional ResNet. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:0aaba6a26891] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] A notable CvT finding is that positional embeddings could be removed without degradation in that design. The authors attribute this simplification to the convolutional structure, which supplies spatial information and makes the architecture more readily adaptable to variable input resolutions. This result is specific to CvT's convolutional token embeddings and projections; it does not show that positional embeddings are unnecessary in the original ViT, whose patch self-attention is otherwise permutation invariant. CvT therefore demonstrates how convolution can alter both efficiency and resolution behavior while preserving attention, but its performance cannot be assigned to either pure ViT or pure CNN mechanisms alone. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:0aaba6a26891] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324]

LeViT represents an efficiency-oriented hybrid rather than a direct dense-prediction backbone. It reintroduces convolutional-network principles into a vision Transformer, especially activation maps with decreasing resolution, and introduces attention bias as a way to integrate positional information. Its stated goal is fast inference image classification, with efficiency measured across hardware platforms rather than reduced to a single accuracy number. LeViT's contribution is a better speed–accuracy operating point in a high-speed classification regime; the abstract reports that at about 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy it is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. That evidence supports fast classification under the paper's hardware and evaluation settings, but it does not make LeViT a direct comparison of original ViT and ResNet for detection or segmentation. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:e4e92da5f487] HVT addresses another plain-ViT efficiency limitation: maintaining a full-length patch sequence throughout inference is redundant and lacks hierarchical representation. It progressively pools visual tokens to shrink sequence length, explicitly drawing an analogy to downsampling CNN feature maps. This permits increases in depth, width, input resolution, or patch-size-related capacity without paying the same full-sequence attention cost, and the paper reports that average-pooled visual tokens contain more discriminative information than a single class token in its empirical setting. HVT is therefore a hierarchical-token classification model. Its mechanism overlaps with CNN downsampling principles, but its results should be interpreted as evidence for token pooling in image classification, not as proof that CNNs and ViTs have equivalent representations. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

ConTNet combines standard Transformer encoders with spatial convolution in a block-level hybrid design. A ConT block contains patch-wise standard Transformer encoder layers followed by a convolution layer; the Transformer models context within patches while the convolution processes the spatial grid. The authors position the design against two limitations: convolutional networks can lack sufficiently large receptive fields for downstream tasks, while vision Transformers can require special training settings or very large pretraining datasets. They claim ConTNet is easier to optimize than trendy visual Transformers and provides strong recognition and transfer behavior. Its evidence belongs to the conv–Transformer pattern category: it deliberately enlarges receptive fields through attention while retaining convolution, rather than isolating the original ViT mechanism. [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:3:aa366e49ea30:claim:164300ccc5ed] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] ViT-CoMer represents the adapted-backbone position: it preserves a plain ViT module so that advanced open-source ViT pretrained weights can be loaded, while adding convolutional multi-scale features rather than redesigning the entire Transformer. Its multi-receptive field feature pyramid supplies local and scale-diverse information that plain ViT lacks, and its CNN–Transformer bidirectional fusion interaction module fuses hierarchical convolutional features with Transformer features. The paper motivates this by two specific plain-ViT weaknesses in dense prediction: insufficient interaction within patches and limited feature-scale diversity. ViT-CoMer is therefore evidence that convolutional branches can compensate for plain ViT's dense-prediction interface while retaining access to ViT pretraining; it is not an unmodified ViT result. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:de8f23109ad5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] The distinction between plain, vision-specific, and adapted backbones is the paper's own paradigm and is useful for interpreting later evidence. A plain backbone can directly use advanced pretrained ViT weights but has limited scale diversity; a vision-specific backbone such as a pyramid Transformer builds multi-scale features into the network but may require structural changes and large-scale retraining; an adapted backbone keeps the original ViT and adds branches that can fuse CNN and Transformer features. ViT-CoMer initializes its ViT module from open-source pretrained weights while randomly initializing the added components. This trade-off between architectural fit and reuse of pretraining is one of the clearest practical differences between replacing a CNN backbone with plain ViT and using a modified Transformer backbone. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:de8f23109ad5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:7267d9b37e07]

A separate line of work analyzes rather than hybridizes the two architectures. Raghu et al. use centered kernel alignment to compare internal representations and find that ViTs have a much more uniform, grid-like similarity structure, while ResNets divide more clearly into lower and higher stages. Cross-model CKA suggests that many lower ResNet layers resemble only the lowest quarter of ViT layers, the upper half of ResNet roughly corresponds to the next third of ViT layers, and the final third of ViT layers has little similar ResNet counterpart in their analysis. Through ablations, they attribute important differences to self-attention's early global aggregation and to residual connections that preserve lower-layer information. This supports a mechanism-level distinction even when both model families produce similar ImageNet predictions. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7935f0e4436d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:c1fb2c740395] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:8754469fe330] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:bc8ff296c103] Broader benchmarking reinforces that architecture choice interacts with pretraining and evaluation target. Battle of the Backbones evaluates a diverse suite of pretrained backbones over classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization, and other tasks using more than 1,500 training runs. Its summary reports that supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-supervised SwinV2-Base, and CLIP ViT-Base are top performers at base scale, while supervised convolutional networks outperform Transformers on most tasks among the models considered. It also reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. These findings concern a modern backbone suite and multiple pretraining algorithms; they should not be reduced to a universal statement that every CNN beats every ViT, nor treated as a controlled test of only the original ViT and ResNet. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:2af299151cfa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be] Finally, the unified dynamic-convolution interpretation offers a design-space bridge rather than a practical merger of architectures. It views vision Transformers as CNNs with dynamic convolutions, allowing Transformer and dynamic ConvNet choices to be compared side by side and transferred between design spaces. Its empirical examples include replacing softmax in Swin-Tiny attention with LayerNorm and ReLU, which the paper reports raises ImageNet top-1 accuracy from 81.13% to 81.56% without added compute, and constructing a depth-wise vision Transformer inspired by depth-wise convolution. This perspective is useful for mechanism analysis and network design, but it does not remove the empirical differences in tokenization, hierarchy, pretraining sensitivity, positional treatment, and dense-prediction interfaces established by the original ViT–CNN comparison. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

The experimental comparison should be read by matched task and training regime rather than as one universal ViT-versus-CNN ranking. The original ViT evidence is strongest for image classification under large-scale pretraining: it decomposes images into non-overlapping patch tokens and applies standard Transformer blocks, and the cited literature describes it as the first pure Transformer to attain state-of-the-art classification against models such as ResNets and EfficientNets when trained on sufficiently large data such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M. That result is not directly comparable to a ResNet trained only on ImageNet-1k, because architecture, pretraining corpus, regularization, and model scale all change at once. A separate ImageNet-1k-from-scratch transformer literature therefore addresses a different question: whether modified or better regularized Transformers can become competitive without the original ViT's large-data regime. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324] [E:arxiv:2103.14899:section:abstract:1:78640899c791:claim:efb5e17d94e6] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be]

The closest dense-prediction comparison in the selected papers is not original ViT versus ResNet but PVT versus established CNN backbones under the same task-specific heads. With RetinaNet on COCO val2017, PVT-Small achieved 40.4 AP versus 36.3 AP for ResNet-50, a 4.1 absolute-point difference at a comparable parameter count; PVT-Large achieved 42.6 AP, 1.6 points above ResNeXt101-64x4d while using 30% fewer parameters according to the paper. These results support the authors' claim that a pyramid Transformer can replace CNN backbones in RetinaNet-style detection in that setup. They do not establish that the plain original ViT would produce the same AP, because PVT adds the progressive shrinking pyramid and spatial-reduction attention specifically to obtain high-resolution multi-scale features at lower resource cost. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:12bdfdbebcf4] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63]

PVT's downstream advantage should be interpreted together with its changed backbone interface. Conventional ResNet and ResNeXt backbones expose stage-wise feature maps that dense heads already consume, whereas the plain ViT is characterized as a single-scale feature extractor with limited scale diversity and weaker suitability for dense prediction. PVT was designed to overcome ViT's low-resolution outputs and high computational and memory cost by learning high-resolution features through a pyramid and reducing attention cost with spatial-reduction attention. Thus, the COCO RetinaNet result compares a vision-specific pyramid Transformer with CNN backbones under a common detector, but it is not a controlled original-ViT/ResNet comparison. Any ranking that transferred the 40.4-to-36.3 AP gap to unmodified ViT would be unsupported. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:15bbb833ac5f] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63]

For adapted plain-ViT dense prediction, ViT-CoMer provides evidence that adding convolutional multi-scale branches can improve the plain-ViT backbone rather than replacing it with a wholly redesigned pyramid Transformer. ViT-CoMer-L is reported to reach 64.3% AP on COCO val2017 without extra detection data such as Objects365 and 62.1% mIoU on ADE20K validation. The paper attributes these gains to a multi-receptive field feature pyramid and CNN–Transformer bidirectional fusion that address plain ViT's limited local interaction and single-scale representation. These are strong results for the adapted-backbone paradigm, but they are not a head-to-head original-ViT versus CNN score: the evaluated model contains both ViT and CNN components, uses advanced open-source ViT pretraining such as DINOv2 in the highlighted setting, and compares against broader state-of-the-art systems rather than isolating convolution as the causal factor. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:de8f23109ad5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:7267d9b37e07]

Hybrid classification results likewise show that introducing convolution can improve the ViT operating point, but the reported numbers belong to the hybrid model. CvT uses hierarchical convolutional token embeddings and convolutional projections, and its paper reports state-of-the-art performance over other Vision Transformers and ResNets on ImageNet-1k with fewer parameters and lower FLOPs; after ImageNet-22k pretraining, CvT-W24 reached 87.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k validation. The paper also reports that positional encoding could be removed in CvT without degradation. Because CvT changes tokenization, hierarchy, projections, and positional treatment, these findings demonstrate a hybrid architecture's performance and efficiency under its training settings; they cannot be interpreted as the original ViT beating ResNet at identical FLOPs or as a generic CNN result. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:0aaba6a26891] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac]

Efficiency comparisons require the hardware, metric, and accuracy target to be kept together. LeViT was explicitly designed for fast inference image classification and combines decreasing-resolution activation maps with attention bias. At approximately 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy, the paper reports that LeViT is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. This supports a speed–accuracy advantage for LeViT over that EfficientNet baseline on the evaluated CPU regime; it does not imply lower FLOPs alone, lower GPU latency, or better dense-prediction performance. HVT supplies a separate classification-efficiency result: progressive token pooling shortens the patch sequence, and with comparable FLOPs the paper reports that HVT outperforms competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100. Those baselines and LeViT's CPU timing are not matched to one another, so the two studies should not be merged into a single efficiency ranking. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:e4e92da5f487] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

ConTNet's evidence targets recognition optimization and downstream transfer through a block-level conv–Transformer pattern. Its ConT-M model is reported to yield around a 3% improvement over ResNet-50 when used with FCOS and Mask R-CNN, according to the paper's abstract. The authors also present ConTNet as easier to optimize than recently proposed visual Transformers and as less dependent on the special training settings or very large pretraining datasets associated with transformer-style vision models. The result is relevant to the CNN–Transformer backbone debate because it combines patch-wise Transformer encoders with spatial convolution, but it is not an original-ViT baseline: both architecture and optimization behavior differ, and the abstract-level report does not provide enough matched detail here to infer a universal AP or accuracy gap. [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:3:aa366e49ea30:claim:164300ccc5ed] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6]

Representation experiments reveal differences that ImageNet accuracy alone does not capture. Using centered kernel alignment, Raghu et al. found that ViTs have a much more uniform, grid-like internal similarity structure, while ResNets separate more clearly into lower and higher stages; lower and higher ViT layers were also more similar to one another than lower and higher ResNet layers. Their cross-model analysis found that many lower ResNet layers corresponded roughly to only the lowest quarter of ViT layers, the upper half of ResNet to approximately the next third of ViT layers, and the final third of ViT layers had little similar ResNet counterpart. Ablations in that study linked the ViT pattern to early global aggregation through self-attention and strong propagation of lower-layer features through residual connections. These are mechanistic measurements on analyzed classification models, not accuracy or latency rankings. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7935f0e4436d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:c1fb2c740395] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:8754469fe330] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:bc8ff296c103]

Large modern backbone benchmarks broaden the empirical picture but mix architectures and pretraining protocols. Battle of the Backbones reports more than 1,500 training runs across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization, and other tasks; among its considered models, supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-supervised SwinV2-Base, and CLIP ViT-Base were top base-scale performers, while supervised convolutional networks performed best on most tasks. The same summary reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count, and that apples-to-apples comparisons at similar pretraining-data scale make self-supervised backbones highly competitive. These findings should not be converted into a direct ResNet-beats-original-ViT verdict because the suite includes ConvNeXt, SwinV2, CLIP, MAE, MoCo, DINO, and other modern systems with different datasets and learning objectives. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:2af299151cfa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be]

Beyond-Backbones further limits the usefulness of a single ImageNet ranking. In a controlled comparative analysis of ConvNet and Vision Transformer architectures across supervised and CLIP training paradigms, models selected for similar ImageNet accuracy and compute still differed in the types of mistakes they made, output calibration, transferability, and feature invariance. Therefore, even when top-1 accuracy and nominal compute are matched, the experimental decision between a ViT-like and convolutional backbone can depend on calibration, robustness, transfer target, and the desired invariances. The selected evidence supports a conditional conclusion: original ViT is a strong large-data global classifier but is not naturally a CNN-style multi-scale dense-prediction backbone; CNN backbones offer mature hierarchical maps and a strong broad-task baseline; and pyramid, hybrid, or adapted Transformers can close or reverse particular downstream gaps only under their stated architectures, pretraining, heads, datasets, and hardware settings. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is that the original ViT's strongest classification evidence does not transfer automatically to the backbone role needed for dense prediction. Plain ViT preserves patch locations and can reason globally, but its native single-scale token sequence lacks the stage-wise, multi-resolution feature interface that detectors and segmenters expect from CNN backbones. PVT explicitly identifies low-resolution outputs, high computational cost, and high memory cost as barriers to porting ViT to pixel-level tasks, while ViT-CoMer separately identifies insufficient inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity. The implication is that downstream users cannot infer detection or segmentation suitability from ImageNet performance alone; they must evaluate spatial resolution, scale diversity, decoder compatibility, token count, and memory together. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63]

A second, closely related problem is the quadratic cost of full self-attention as image resolution grows. A conventional CNN controls dense-feature cost through strided convolution and stage-wise downsampling, whereas maintaining a full-length ViT patch sequence creates larger attention maps and can make high-resolution inference expensive. PVT responds with a progressive shrinking pyramid and spatial-reduction attention, and HVT responds by progressively pooling tokens. These are credible mitigations, but they also change the architecture and its outputs; they do not make the original plain ViT free of the resolution–memory trade-off. FLOP reductions likewise should not be treated as latency reductions unless the relevant hardware and runtime are measured. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:15bbb833ac5f] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63]

The third problem is pretraining dependence. The original pure-Transformer recipe became competitive with strong CNN classifiers when large datasets such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M were available, while ConTNet notes that vision Transformers can be sensitive to learning rate, training epochs, optimizer, augmentation, and other settings. Battle of the Backbones similarly reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and to parameter count. This makes model comparisons conditional: a ViT pretrained on a huge corpus, a CNN supervised on ImageNet-1k, and a self-supervised backbone answer different empirical questions. The practical limitation is that reproducing ViT's best classification regime may require data, compute, and regularization unavailable for a specialized vision task. [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be] [E:arxiv:2103.14899:section:abstract:1:78640899c791:claim:efb5e17d94e6]

Fourth, architectural modification often creates a pretraining-reuse trade-off. Vision-specific pyramid Transformers can build the hierarchical features needed for dense prediction, but changing the plain ViT structure can prevent direct reuse of existing powerful ViT checkpoints and may require large-scale retraining. ViT-CoMer's adapted design illustrates the alternative: keep the original ViT module so open-source pretrained weights can be loaded, add convolutional multi-scale branches, and randomly initialize the added components. This improves task fit but introduces new modules, fusion complexity, and a training burden for the CNN branch. The unresolved practical issue is therefore not only how to obtain multi-scale features, but whether doing so preserves the value of already learned ViT representations. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:de8f23109ad5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:7267d9b37e07] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b]

Fifth, ViTs and CNNs can make different errors even when headline accuracy and compute are similar. Comparative behavioral work finds that matched ConvNet and Vision Transformer models can differ in mistake types, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance across supervised and CLIP training paradigms. This means ImageNet top-1 accuracy is an insufficient selection criterion for a backbone: a model with the same classification score may be worse calibrated, less robust out of distribution, or less transferable to the target sensor domain. The implication is that deployment-oriented backbone comparison needs task-specific calibration, robustness, and transfer evaluations rather than a single leaderboard number. [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:641138c80176] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:2af299151cfa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be]

Sixth, the internal-representation evidence shows that similar predictions do not imply similar visual processing. ViTs exhibit a more uniform, grid-like representation across layers, with greater similarity between lower and higher layers, whereas ResNets separate more clearly into stages. The same analysis attributes important parts of this pattern to early global aggregation by self-attention and to strong feature propagation through ViT residual connections. This creates an open interpretation problem for model replacement: a ViT may preserve spatial information and classify accurately without learning the same hierarchical stage structure as a CNN. Downstream heads designed around CNN stage semantics may therefore behave differently even when attached successfully. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7935f0e4436d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:8754469fe330] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:c1fb2c740395] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:bc8ff296c103]

Seventh, locality and global context remain a genuine trade-off rather than a solved choice. Ordinary CNN layers impose local receptive fields, shared weights, and spatial subsampling, which help encode local visual structure efficiently but require depth or specialized modules to model very long-range relations. ViT attention directly mixes distant patch tokens, but the original design lacks convolution's built-in local processing and progressive hierarchy. Hybrid models such as CvT and ConTNet show that convolutional tokenization, convolutional projections, or block-level convolution can add local context, but they also make it impossible to attribute a result purely to either self-attention or convolution. The open problem is how to obtain local bias and adaptive global mixing without paying the full cost, retraining cost, or confounding both mechanisms in evaluation. [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:3:aa366e49ea30:claim:164300ccc5ed] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324]

Eighth, variable-resolution deployment remains difficult because positional treatment and token density interact. The original ViT relies on positional embeddings in a permutation-invariant attention architecture, whereas CvT reports that its convolutional projections and embeddings allow positional encoding to be removed without degradation, simplifying higher-resolution use. That finding is design-specific and should not be generalized to plain ViT. High-resolution multimodal and edge systems also face excessive visual tokens, quadratic complexity, latency, and memory pressure; proposed responses include hierarchical ConvNeXt encoders, token compression, model splitting, and class-wise pruning. These systems address deployment constraints after architecture choice and do not establish that the original ViT has a native resolution-robust solution. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:72b69999401c] [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:9bbd47dc137e] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:0aaba6a26891] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:6f8729d848c1]

Finally, the field lacks a clean universal ranking because benchmark suites mix architecture, pretraining objective, dataset scale, model size, task head, and hardware. Battle of the Backbones finds supervised convolutional networks strongest on most tasks among the models it considered, yet also reports top performance for specific supervised SwinV2 and CLIP ViT variants and competitive self-supervised models in apples-to-apples dataset-scale comparisons. PVT and ViT-CoMer show strong dense-prediction results for redesigned or adapted Transformers, while LeViT and HVT address particular efficiency regimes. These findings are complementary, not interchangeable: the original ViT, ResNet-like CNNs, hybrid models, and modern pretrained backbones must be compared under matched tasks and settings before one can claim general superiority. ## Conclusion

For a system choosing a backbone, the central trade-off is between ViT's direct global token mixing and the CNN's built-in locality, hierarchy, and dense-prediction interface. The original ViT preserves patch locations and can aggregate information globally, but its equal-resolution token sequence is not a conventional feature pyramid; CNN backbones expose stage-wise maps that detectors and segmenters already consume, although ordinary convolutional blocks do not perform ViT-style global token mixing. Consequently, ImageNet success alone does not establish that plain ViT replaces ResNet for detection or segmentation.
