## Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is that the original ViT's strongest classification evidence does not transfer automatically to the backbone role needed for dense prediction. Plain ViT preserves patch locations and can reason globally, but its native single-scale token sequence lacks the stage-wise, multi-resolution feature interface that detectors and segmenters expect from CNN backbones. PVT explicitly identifies low-resolution outputs, high computational cost, and high memory cost as barriers to porting ViT to pixel-level tasks, while ViT-CoMer separately identifies insufficient inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity. The implication is that downstream users cannot infer detection or segmentation suitability from ImageNet performance alone; they must evaluate spatial resolution, scale diversity, decoder compatibility, token count, and memory together. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63]

A second, closely related problem is the quadratic cost of full self-attention as image resolution grows. A conventional CNN controls dense-feature cost through strided convolution and stage-wise downsampling, whereas maintaining a full-length ViT patch sequence creates larger attention maps and can make high-resolution inference expensive. PVT responds with a progressive shrinking pyramid and spatial-reduction attention, and HVT responds by progressively pooling tokens. These are credible mitigations, but they also change the architecture and its outputs; they do not make the original plain ViT free of the resolution–memory trade-off. FLOP reductions likewise should not be treated as latency reductions unless the relevant hardware and runtime are measured. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:15bbb833ac5f] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63]

The third problem is pretraining dependence. The original pure-Transformer recipe became competitive with strong CNN classifiers when large datasets such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M were available, while ConTNet notes that vision Transformers can be sensitive to learning rate, training epochs, optimizer, augmentation, and other settings. Battle of the Backbones similarly reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and to parameter count. This makes model comparisons conditional: a ViT pretrained on a huge corpus, a CNN supervised on ImageNet-1k, and a self-supervised backbone answer different empirical questions. The practical limitation is that reproducing ViT's best classification regime may require data, compute, and regularization unavailable for a specialized vision task. [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be] [E:arxiv:2103.14899:section:abstract:1:78640899c791:claim:efb5e17d94e6]

Fourth, architectural modification often creates a pretraining-reuse trade-off. Vision-specific pyramid Transformers can build the hierarchical features needed for dense prediction, but changing the plain ViT structure can prevent direct reuse of existing powerful ViT checkpoints and may require large-scale retraining. ViT-CoMer's adapted design illustrates the alternative: keep the original ViT module so open-source pretrained weights can be loaded, add convolutional multi-scale branches, and randomly initialize the added components. This improves task fit but introduces new modules, fusion complexity, and a training burden for the CNN branch. The unresolved practical issue is therefore not only how to obtain multi-scale features, but whether doing so preserves the value of already learned ViT representations. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:de8f23109ad5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:7267d9b37e07] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b]

Fifth, ViTs and CNNs can make different errors even when headline accuracy and compute are similar. Comparative behavioral work finds that matched ConvNet and Vision Transformer models can differ in mistake types, calibration, transferability, and feature invariance across supervised and CLIP training paradigms. This means ImageNet top-1 accuracy is an insufficient selection criterion for a backbone: a model with the same classification score may be worse calibrated, less robust out of distribution, or less transferable to the target sensor domain. The implication is that deployment-oriented backbone comparison needs task-specific calibration, robustness, and transfer evaluations rather than a single leaderboard number. [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:641138c80176] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:2af299151cfa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be]

Sixth, the internal-representation evidence shows that similar predictions do not imply similar visual processing. ViTs exhibit a more uniform, grid-like representation across layers, with greater similarity between lower and higher layers, whereas ResNets separate more clearly into stages. The same analysis attributes important parts of this pattern to early global aggregation by self-attention and to strong feature propagation through ViT residual connections. This creates an open interpretation problem for model replacement: a ViT may preserve spatial information and classify accurately without learning the same hierarchical stage structure as a CNN. Downstream heads designed around CNN stage semantics may therefore behave differently even when attached successfully. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7935f0e4436d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:8754469fe330] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:c1fb2c740395] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:bc8ff296c103]

Seventh, locality and global context remain a genuine trade-off rather than a solved choice. Ordinary CNN layers impose local receptive fields, shared weights, and spatial subsampling, which help encode local visual structure efficiently but require depth or specialized modules to model very long-range relations. ViT attention directly mixes distant patch tokens, but the original design lacks convolution's built-in local processing and progressive hierarchy. Hybrid models such as CvT and ConTNet show that convolutional tokenization, convolutional projections, or block-level convolution can add local context, but they also make it impossible to attribute a result purely to either self-attention or convolution. The open problem is how to obtain local bias and adaptive global mixing without paying the full cost, retraining cost, or confounding both mechanisms in evaluation. [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:3:aa366e49ea30:claim:164300ccc5ed] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:f529d357d324]

Eighth, variable-resolution deployment remains difficult because positional treatment and token density interact. The original ViT relies on positional embeddings in a permutation-invariant attention architecture, whereas CvT reports that its convolutional projections and embeddings allow positional encoding to be removed without degradation, simplifying higher-resolution use. That finding is design-specific and should not be generalized to plain ViT. High-resolution multimodal and edge systems also face excessive visual tokens, quadratic complexity, latency, and memory pressure; proposed responses include hierarchical ConvNeXt encoders, token compression, model splitting, and class-wise pruning. These systems address deployment constraints after architecture choice and do not establish that the original ViT has a native resolution-robust solution. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:c2a99460bd76:claim:1b4fa799457c] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:72b69999401c] [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:9bbd47dc137e] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:0aaba6a26891] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:6f8729d848c1]

Finally, the field lacks a clean universal ranking because benchmark suites mix architecture, pretraining objective, dataset scale, model size, task head, and hardware. Battle of the Backbones finds supervised convolutional networks strongest on most tasks among the models it considered, yet also reports top performance for specific supervised SwinV2 and CLIP ViT variants and competitive self-supervised models in apples-to-apples dataset-scale comparisons. PVT and ViT-CoMer show strong dense-prediction results for redesigned or adapted Transformers, while LeViT and HVT address particular efficiency regimes. These findings are complementary, not interchangeable: the original ViT, ResNet-like CNNs, hybrid models, and modern pretrained backbones must be compared under matched tasks and settings before one can claim general superiority. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:2af299151cfa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:ecfb794852be] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:e4e92da5f487] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

## Conclusion

For a system choosing a backbone, the central trade-off is between ViT's direct global token mixing and the CNN's built-in locality, hierarchy, and dense-prediction interface. The original ViT preserves patch locations and can aggregate information globally, but its equal-resolution token sequence is not a conventional feature pyramid; CNN backbones expose stage-wise maps that detectors and segmenters already consume, although ordinary convolutional blocks do not perform ViT-style global token mixing. Consequently, ImageNet success alone does not establish that plain ViT replaces ResNet for detection or segmentation. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:06630e24af5f] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:bc8ff296c103] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7935f0e4436d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:c1fb2c740395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:cfff705eb04f] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:12bdfdbebcf4] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:16e1b0129d63] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:4e411117582d] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:2:0711a86ccc19:claim:21a4340ba3ac] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:2:0eca0ad691e2:claim:932e44907c51] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:d91d94488b7b] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:8754469fe330]

Strong downstream Transformer results should be assigned to the modified architecture and recipe. PVT's 40.4 versus 36.3 AP RetinaNet advantage over ResNet-50 reflects a pyramid Transformer with spatial-reduction attention, and ViT-CoMer's reported 64.3% COCO AP and 62.1% ADE20K mIoU reflect an adapted ViT with convolutional multi-scale branches and fusion. CvT, LeViT, HVT, and ConTNet similarly address hierarchy, locality, resolution, efficiency, or optimization rather than testing the unmodified ViT. The practical answer is therefore not a blanket ranking: use matched task, head, pretraining data, model scale, and hardware comparisons, while treating CNNs as mature hierarchical baselines and plain ViT as a globally attentive classifier whose backbone use may require adaptation. claim_records.text: HIRI-ViT upgrades prevalent four-stage ViT to five-stage ViT tailored for high-resolution inputs.

HIRI-ViT decomposes typical CNN operations into two parallel CNN branches: one high-resolution branch directly takes primary high-resolution features as inputs with less convolution operations, and the other low-resolution branch first performs down-sampling then utilizes more convolution operations over low-resolution features.
Experiments on ImageNet-1K recognition task and COCO, ADE20K dense prediction tasks demonstrate the superiority of HIRI-ViT.

Under comparable computational cost of approximately 5.0 GFLOPs, HIRI-ViT achieves 84.3% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 448×448 inputs, which is 0.9% higher than iFormer-S's 83.4% Top-1 accuracy with 224×224 inputs.

Existing high-resolution ViT backbones including HRViT and HRFormer still limit inputs to 224×224 resolution, and most hybrid backbones can be directly scaled up to higher resolution such as 384×384 but suffer from sharply increased computation cost.

IRDS-a, adopted for downsampling in the first two high-resolution stages, first uses a strided 3×3 convolution to expand dimension and reduce spatial size, then uses a 1×1 convolution to shrink channel dimension.

IRDS-b, leveraged for the last two downsampling layers, is similar to inverted residual block, with normalization and activation operations applied only after the first convolution, and extra downsampling shortcuts are added to stabilize training.

HIRI-ViT constructs three variants of different model sizes: HIRI-ViT-S (small), HIRI-ViT-B (base), and HIRI-ViT-L (large), following the basic network configuration of existing CNN+ViT hybrid backbones.

The entire HIRI-ViT architecture is composed of one HR-stem layer and five stages: the first two high-resolution stages use light-weight High Resolution blocks to avoid huge computational overhead, the third stage uses only CFFN blocks to handle middle-resolution feature maps, and the last two low-resolution stages employ Transformer blocks similar to conventional Vision Transformer.
When directly enlarging Swin Transformer's input resolution from 224×224 to 384×384, the top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K evidently changes alongside sharply increased computational costs.

evidence_items.claim_text: The entire HIRI-ViT architecture is composed of one HR-stem layer and five stages: the first two high-resolution stages use light-weight High Resolution blocks to avoid huge computational overhead, the third stage uses only CFFN blocks to handle middle-resolution feature maps, and the last two low-resolution stages employ Transformer blocks similar to conventional Vision Transformer.

evidence_items.paper_title: HIRI-ViT: Scaling Vision Transformer with High Resolution Inputs
evidence_items.claim_text: When directly enlarging Swin Transformer's input resolution from 224×224 to 384×384, the top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K evidently changes alongside sharply increased computational costs.

claim_records.text: CrossViT is a dual-branch transformer that processes small-patch and large-patch tokens with two separate branches of different computational complexity, and fuses these tokens purely by attention multiple times to complement each other.

The cross-attention based token fusion module in CrossViT uses a single token for each branch as a query to exchange information with other branches, requiring only linear time for both computational and memory complexity instead of quadratic time.
On the ImageNet1K dataset, with some architectural changes, CrossViT outperforms DeiT by a large margin of 2% with a small to moderate increase in FLOPs and model parameters.
CrossViT's approach performs better than or on par with several concurrent works on vision transformer, in addition to efficient CNN models.

CrossViT's dual-branch transformer creates a non-patch token as an agent in each transformer branch to exchange information with the other branch by attention, allowing for linear-time generation of the attention map in fusion instead of quadratic time.
CrossViT demonstrates comparable results with EfficientNet with regards to accuracy, throughput and model parameters.

Vision Transformer (ViT) is the first convolution-free transformer-based method to match or even surpass CNNs for image classification, and requires very large datasets such as ImageNet21K and JFT300M for training.
DeiT shows that data augmentation and model regularization can enable training of high-performance ViT models with fewer data.
Multi-scale feature representations have proven beneficial for many vision tasks, but their applicability for vision transformer remains a novel and largely under-addressed problem.

BoTNet replaced the spatial convolutions with global self-attention in the final three bottleneck blocks of a ResNet resulting in models that achieve strong performance for image classification on ImageNet benchmark.

claim_records.text: With a comparable number of parameters, RetinaNet+PVT achieves 40.4 AP on the COCO dataset, surpassing RetinaNet+ResNet50 (36.3 AP) by 4.1 absolute AP.
PVT can be trained on dense partitions of the image to achieve high output resolution, and uses a progressive shrinking pyramid to reduce computations of large feature maps.
PVT inherits the advantages from both CNN and Transformer, making it a unified backbone in various vision tasks without convolutions by simply replacing CNN backbones.
PVT-T achieves 36.7 AP with 23.0M parameters on COCO val2017 using RetinaNet for object detection.
PVT-S achieves 40.4 AP with 34.2M parameters on COCO val2017 using RetinaNet for object detection.
PVT-M achieves 41.9 AP with 53.9M parameters on COCO val2017 using RetinaNet for object detection.
PVT-L achieves 42.6 AP with 71.1M parameters on COCO val2017 using RetinaNet for object detection.
R50 (ResNet50) achieves 36.3 AP with 37.7M parameters on COCO val2017 using RetinaNet for object detection.
ViT-S/32 achieves 31.7 AP with 60.8M parameters on COCO val2017 using RetinaNet for object detection.

PVT takes fine-grained image patches of 4×4 pixels per patch as input to learn high-resolution representation, introduces a progressive shrinking pyramid to reduce sequence length as the network deepens, and adopts a spatial-reduction attention (SRA) layer to further reduce resource consumption when learning high-resolution features.

PVT always produces a global receptive field, which is more suitable for detection and segmentation compared to traditional CNN backbones that have local receptive fields increasing with network depth.
Combining PVT and DETR constructs an end-to-end object detection system without convolutions and handcrafted components such as dense anchors and non-maximum suppression (NMS).
PVT-Large achieves 42.6 AP, which is 1.6 points better than ResNeXt101-64x4d, with 30% less parameters.

claim_records.text: ViT-CoMer-L achieves 64.3% AP on COCO val2017 without extra training data.
ViT-CoMer-L achieves 62.1% mIoU on ADE20K val.

ViT-CoMer injects spatial pyramid multi-receptive field convolutional features into the ViT architecture to alleviate the problems of limited local information interaction and single-feature representation in ViT.

ViT-CoMer proposes a simple and efficient CNN-Transformer bidirectional fusion interaction module that performs multi-scale fusion across hierarchical features, which is beneficial for handling dense prediction tasks.
ViT-CoMer-T achieves 47.1 APb with 29M parameters on COCO val2017 using Mask R-CNN for object detection, with ImageNet-1K pre-training.
ViT-CoMer-S achieves 48.8 APb with 50M parameters on COCO val2017 using Mask R-CNN for object detection, with ImageNet-1K pre-training.
ViT-CoMer-S† achieves 52.1 APb with 50M parameters on COCO val2017 using Mask R-CNN for object detection, with advanced pre-trained weights.
ViT-CoMer-B achieves 50.2 APb with 129M parameters on COCO val2017 using Mask R-CNN for object detection, with ImageNet-1K pre-training.
ViT-CoMer-B† achieves 54.2 APb with 129M parameters on COCO val2017 using Mask R-CNN for object detection, with advanced pre-trained weights.
ViT-CoMer-L† achieves 55.9 APb with 363M parameters on COCO val2017 using Mask R-CNN for object detection, with advanced pre-trained weights.

The adapted backbone paradigm integrates the advantages of both CNN and transformer, can directly load advanced pre-training and achieve fusion interaction between multi-scale convolutional features and transformer features, which is beneficial for dense predictions.
In the weight initialization process of ViT-CoMer, the ViT module directly uses the open-source pre-training, and the rest use random initialization.
ViT-CoMer-L with advanced pre-training achieves 64.3% AP, which is the best record on COCO val2017 without training on extra detection data such as Objects365.
ViT-CoMer-L attains 62.1% mIoU on the ADE20K val, which is comparable with SOTA methods.

PVT constructs a feature pyramid structure to address the limitations of single-scale features in ViT, which simplifies the structure of the transformer and effectively reduces the computational complexity.

claim_records.text: BoB benchmarks a diverse suite of pretrained models, including vision-language models, self-supervised learning trained models, and the Stable Diffusion backbone, across computer vision tasks ranging from classification to object detection to OOD generalization.
BoB's comprehensive analysis was conducted on more than 1500 training runs.

fact_fields.method: comprehensive analysis of BoB benchmark results

claim_records.text: Among the models considered in BoB, convolutional neural networks pretrained in a supervised fashion on large training sets still perform best on most tasks.
In apples-to-apples comparisons on the same architectures and similarly sized pretraining datasets, SSL backbones are highly competitive.

Across BoB's comprehensive evaluations spanning tasks, datasets, and settings including ID and OOD, supervised ConvNeXt-Base, supervised SwinV2-Base trained using ImageNet-21k, and CLIP ViT-Base come out on top.
Among smaller backbones evaluated in BoB, ConvNeXt-Tiny and SwinV2-Tiny emerge victorious, followed by DINO ViT-Small.
High-performance convolutional networks pretrained via supervised learning outperform transformers on the majority of tasks considered in BoB.

The observed superiority of supervised pretraining in BoB occurs because such models are often trained on larger datasets; in apples-to-apples comparisons on the same dataset scale, SSL models outperform their supervised counterparts.
ViTs are more sensitive to the amount of pretraining data and the number of parameters than CNNs.
Performance across tasks is strongly correlated in BoB, such that top-performing backbones tend to be universally good across tasks and settings.

BoB compares many popular publicly available pretrained checkpoints as well as randomly initialized baselines on downstream tasks including image classification on natural, medical, and satellite images, object detection and segmentation, out-of-distribution generalization, and image retrieval.

claim_records.text: CvT improves ViT performance and efficiency by introducing convolutions into ViT via two primary modifications: a hierarchy of Transformers with a new convolutional token embedding, and a convolutional Transformer block leveraging a convolutional projection.

fact_fields.method: architecture design: convolutional token embedding + convolutional projection in hierarchical Transformer

claim_records.text: CvT achieves state-of-the-art performance over other Vision Transformers and ResNets on ImageNet-1k, with fewer parameters and lower FLOPs.
Pre-trained on ImageNet-22k, CvT-W24 obtains a top-1 accuracy of 87.7% on the ImageNet-1k validation set.

fact_fields.method: large-scale pretraining followed by evaluation on validation set

claim_records.text: The positional encoding, a crucial component in existing Vision Transformers, can be safely removed in CvT without performance degradation, simplifying design for higher resolution vision tasks.
The convolutional projection in CvT employs an s×s depth-wise separable convolution operation on a 2D-reshaped token map, replacing the linear projection prior to every self-attention block.
Using convolution stride to subsample key and value matrices in CvT improves efficiency by 4× or more with minimal degradation of performance.

fact_fields.method: stride-based subsampling of key and value matrices via convolutional projection

claim_records.text: CvT improves performance compared to CNN-based models (e.g. ResNet) and prior Transformer-based models (e.g. ViT, DeiT) while utilizing fewer FLOPs and parameters when pre-trained with ImageNet-1k.
CvT can drop the positional embedding for tokens without any degradation to model performance, making it readily capable of accommodating variable resolutions of input images.

The Vision Transformer (ViT) is the first pure Transformer architecture to attain state-of-the-art performance on image classification when training data is large enough (i.e. on ImageNet-22k, JFT-300M).

fact_fields.method: literature summary of prior ViT results

claim_records.text: ViT decomposes each image into a sequence of non-overlapping patch tokens with fixed length, then applies multiple standard Transformer layers consisting of Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and Position-wise Feed-forward (FFN) modules.

The convolutional token embedding in CvT performs an overlapping convolution operation with stride on a 2D-reshaped token map, followed by layer normalization, enabling spatial downsampling while increasing feature map dimensions across stages.
CvT incorporates convolutions into two core sections of ViT: a hierarchical multi-stage structure with convolutional token embedding, and convolutional projection within each Transformer block.

claim_records.text: FCDM-XL achieves competitive performance with 7.5× fewer training steps than DiT-XL/2 at 512×512 resolution while using only 50% of DiT-XL/2's FLOPs.

fact_fields.method: FCDM (Fully Convolutional Diffusion Model) with ConvNeXt-like backbone

claim_records.text: FCDM-XL can be trained on a 4-GPU system, demonstrating exceptional training efficiency of the FCDM architecture.

FCDM-S achieves 48.5 FID after 400K training steps, using 3G FLOPs and reaching 2687 it/s throughput, compared to DiT-S/2's 68.4 FID, 6G FLOPs, and 1234 it/s throughput at the same 400K training steps.

FCDM-B achieves 26.2 FID after 400K training steps, using 12G FLOPs and reaching 1002 it/s throughput, compared to DiT-B/2's 43.5 FID, 23G FLOPs, and 380.1 it/s throughput at the same 400K training steps.

FCDM-L achieves 13.8 FID after 400K training steps, using 48G FLOPs and reaching 381.3 it/s throughput, compared to DiT-L/2's 23.3 FID, 81G FLOPs, and 114.6 it/s throughput at the same 400K training steps.

FCDM-XL achieves 10.7 FID after 400K training steps, using 65G FLOPs and reaching 272.7 it/s throughput, compared to DiT-XL/2's 19.5 FID, 119G FLOPs, and 80.5 it/s throughput at the same 400K training steps.

FCDM-XL achieves 7.9 FID after 1M training steps, using 65G FLOPs and reaching 272.7 it/s throughput, compared to DiT-XL/2's 9.6 FID after 7M training steps, using 119G FLOPs and reaching 80.5 it/s throughput.
When scaled to match DiT model parameter counts, FCDM models require approximately 50% fewer FLOPs than their DiT counterparts.

The proposed FCDM revived ConvNeXt backbone achieves superior generative performance and higher computational efficiency than prior convolutional diffusion models DiC and DiCo.

claim_records.text: The proposed end-to-end text recognition framework combines ResNet and Vision Transformer backbones with Deformable Convolutions, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Conditional Random Fields (CRF).

The framework substitutes standard convolution layers in the third and fourth blocks with Deformable Convolutions, leverages adaptive dropout for regularization, and incorporates CRF for more refined sequence modeling.
The proposed method achieves 97.32% accuracy on the IC13 benchmark dataset.
The proposed method achieves 58.26% accuracy on the IC15 benchmark dataset.
The proposed method achieves 88.10% accuracy on the SVT benchmark dataset.
The proposed method achieves 74.13% accuracy on the IIIT5K benchmark dataset.
The proposed method achieves 82.17% accuracy on the SVTP benchmark dataset.
The proposed method achieves 66.67% accuracy on the CUTE80 benchmark dataset.
The proposed method achieves an average accuracy of 77.77% across the six benchmark datasets IC13, IC15, SVT, IIIT5K, SVTP, and CUTE80.

claim_records.text: The routine of the current ViT model is to maintain a full-length patch sequence during inference, which is redundant and lacks hierarchical representation.

Hierarchical Visual Transformer (HVT) progressively pools visual tokens to shrink the sequence length and hence reduces the computational cost, analogous to the feature maps downsampling in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).

HVT brings a benefit that we can increase the model capacity by scaling dimensions of depth/width/resolution/patch size without introducing extra computational complexity due to the reduced sequence length.
The average pooled visual tokens contain more discriminative information than the single class token.
With comparable FLOPs, HVT outperforms the competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100 datasets for the image classification task.

claim_records.text: Vision Transformers' inherent reliance on sequential input enforces the manual partitioning of images into patch sequences, which disrupts the image's inherent structural and semantic continuity.

Patternformer adaptively converts images to pattern sequences for Transformer input by employing a Convolutional Neural Network to extract various patterns from the input image, with each channel representing a unique pattern that is fed into the succeeding Transformer as a visual token.
By enabling the network to optimize these patterns, each pattern concentrates on its local region of interest, thereby preserving its intrinsic structural and semantic information.
Only employing the vanilla ResNet and Transformer, Patternformer has accomplished state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
Only employing the vanilla ResNet and Transformer, Patternformer has achieved competitive results on ImageNet.

claim_records.text: ConvLLaVA employs ConvNeXt, a hierarchical backbone, as the visual encoder of LMM to replace Vision Transformer (ViT).
ConvLLaVA compresses high-resolution images into information-rich visual features, effectively preventing the generation of excessive visual tokens.
The low-resolution pretrained ConvNeXt underperforms when directly applied on high resolution, so it is updated to bridge the gap as one of the two critical optimizations for ConvLLaVA.

ConvNeXt's original compression ratio is inadequate for much higher resolution inputs, so a successive stage is trained to further compress visual tokens and reduce redundancy as the second critical optimization for ConvLLaVA.
The two optimizations enable ConvLLaVA to support inputs of 1536x1536 resolution generating only 576 visual tokens, capable of handling images of arbitrary aspect ratios.
Experimental results demonstrate that ConvLLaVA achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art models on mainstream benchmarks.

claim_records.text: A competitive convolution-free transformer is produced by training on ImageNet only, trained on a single computer in less than 3 days.
The reference vision transformer with 86M parameters achieves top-1 accuracy of 83.1% (single-crop evaluation) on ImageNet with no external data.
A teacher-student strategy specific to transformers is introduced, relying on a distillation token ensuring that the student learns from the teacher through attention.
Token-based distillation, especially when using a convnet as a teacher, leads to results competitive with convnets on ImageNet, where up to 85.2% accuracy is obtained.
Token-based distillation with a convnet teacher also yields results competitive with convnets when transferring to other tasks.

claim_records.text: S2AFormer is an efficient Vision Transformer architecture featuring novel Strip Self-Attention (SSA).
S2AFormer uses Hybrid Perception Blocks (HPBs) to integrate the local perception capabilities of CNNs with the global context modeling of Transformer's attention mechanisms.
Strip Self-Attention (SSA) reduces the spatial dimensions of K and V while compressing the channel dimensions of Q and K.
The SSA design significantly reduces computational overhead while preserving accuracy, striking an optimal balance between efficiency and effectiveness.

claim_records.text: A Vision Transformer (ViT) is a simple neural architecture amenable to serve several computer vision tasks.
ViTs have limited built-in architectural priors, in contrast to more recent architectures that incorporate priors either about the input data or of specific tasks.
Recent works show that ViTs benefit from self-supervised pre-training, in particular BerT-like pre-training like BeiT.
The DeiT III supervised training procedure for ViTs builds upon and simplifies a recipe introduced for training ResNet-50.
The DeiT III procedure includes a new simple data-augmentation procedure with only 3 augmentations, closer to the practice in self-supervised learning.

The DeiT III procedure outperforms by a large margin previous fully supervised training recipes for ViT on image classification (ImageNet-1k with and without pre-training on ImageNet-21k), transfer learning and semantic segmentation.
The performance of ViT trained with the DeiT III supervision procedure is comparable to that of more recent architectures.
The DeiT III results could serve as better baselines for recent self-supervised approaches demonstrated on ViT.

claim_records.text: Modern vision systems' performance degrades remarkably quickly when given new tasks with very little data, such as new classes in a classification problem or a domain shift in the input.

Neural network representations underpinning modern vision systems are subject to supervision collapse, whereby they lose any information that is not necessary for performing the training task, including information that may be necessary for transfer to new tasks or domains.
Employing self-supervised learning is proposed as a method to encourage general-purpose features that transfer better, mitigating the supervision collapse problem.

CrossTransformers is a novel Transformer-based neural network architecture that can take a small number of labeled images and an unlabeled query, find coarse spatial correspondence between the query and the labeled images, and then infer class membership by computing distances between spatially-corresponding features.

claim_records.text: The feature maps of vision encoders are fundamental to myriad modern AI tasks, ranging from core perception algorithms (e.g. semantic segmentation, object detection, depth perception, etc.) to modern multimodal understanding in vision-language models (VLMs).
The current frontier of general purpose vision backbones in computer vision is Vision Transformers (ViT), typically trained using contrastive loss (e.g. CLIP).
Most off-the-shelf ViTs, particularly CLIP, are inflexibly low resolution, typically running at 224×224px, while their "high-resolution" versions are around 378-448px but still inflexible.

FeatSharp is a novel method to coherently and cheaply upsample the feature maps of low-resolution vision encoders while picking up on fine-grained details that would otherwise be lost due to resolution.
FeatSharp's effectiveness is demonstrated on core perception tasks as well as within agglomerative model training using RADIO as a way of providing richer targets for distillation.

claim_records.text: ViT achieves inferior performance to CNNs when trained from scratch on a midsize dataset like ImageNet.
The simple tokenization of input images in ViT fails to model important local structure such as edges and lines among neighboring pixels, leading to low training sample efficiency.
The redundant attention backbone design of ViT leads to limited feature richness for fixed computation budgets and limited training samples.

T2T-ViT incorporates a layer-wise Tokens-to-Token (T2T) transformation that progressively structurizes images to tokens by recursively aggregating neighboring Tokens into one Token, enabling local structure modeling and reducing token length.

fact_fields.method: Tokens-To-Token Vision Transformer (T2T-ViT) with layer-wise Tokens-to-Token transformation

claim_records.text: T2T-ViT uses an efficient deep-narrow backbone structure for vision transformers, motivated by CNN architecture design after empirical study.
T2T-ViT reduces the parameter count and MACs of vanilla ViT by half while achieving more than 3.0% improvement when trained from scratch on ImageNet.
T2T-ViT outperforms ResNets and achieves comparable performance with MobileNets by directly training on ImageNet.
T2T-ViT with comparable size to ResNet50 (21.5M parameters) achieves 83.3% top1 accuracy at image resolution 384×384 on ImageNet.
The code for T2T-ViT is available at https://github.com/yitu-opensource/T2T-ViT.

claim_records.text: Dual Path Network (DPN) is a simple, highly efficient and modularized network for image classification with a new topology of connection paths internally.
ResNet enables feature re-usage while DenseNet enables new features exploration, as revealed by their equivalence within the HORNN framework.
The proposed Dual Path Network shares common features while maintaining the flexibility to explore new features through dual path architectures.
Extensive experiments on ImagNet-1k, Places365 and PASCAL VOC demonstrate superior performance of DPN over state-of-the-arts.
On the ImagNet-1k dataset, a shallow DPN surpasses the best ResNeXt-101(64x4d) with 26% smaller model size, 25% less computational cost and 8% lower memory consumption.
On ImagNet-1k, DPN-131 further pushes the state-of-the-art single model performance with about 2 times faster training speed.
Experiments on Places365, PASCAL VOC detection and PASCAL VOC segmentation datasets demonstrate DPN's consistently better performance than DenseNet, ResNet and ResNeXt over various applications.

assertions.source_quote: The original ViT and CNN backbones differ mainly in backbone interface and data dependence, not just accuracy. Plain ViT embeds fixed image patches and applies global self-attention; its strongest early classification results required large-scale pretraining such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M. ResNet-like CNNs use local shared kernels and expose progressively downsampled, multi-stage maps suited to established detection and segmentation heads. Full attention also costs quadratically more as token count rises. Dense-prediction evidence mostly concerns modified Transformers: RetinaNet with PVT-Small reached 40.4 AP on COCO val2017 versus 36.3 AP with ResNet-50, but PVT adds a pyramid and spatial-reduction attention, so this is not a plain-ViT result. Modern benchmarks likewise mix architectures and pretraining; Battle of the Backbones reports supervised CNNs strongest on most considered tasks and greater ViT sensitivity to data and scale. assertions.source_quote: The original ViT and CNN backbones differ mainly in backbone interface and data dependence, not just accuracy. Plain ViT embeds fixed image patches and applies global self-attention; its strongest early classification results required large-scale pretraining such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M. ResNet-like CNNs use local shared kernels and expose progressively downsampled, multi-stage maps suited to established detection and segmentation heads. Full attention also costs quadratically more as token count rises. Dense-prediction evidence mostly concerns modified Transformers: RetinaNet with PVT-Small reached 40.4 AP on COCO val2017 versus 36.3 AP with ResNet-50, but PVT adds a pyramid and spatial-reduction attention, so this is not a plain-ViT result. Modern benchmarks likewise mix architectures and pretraining; Battle of the Backbones reports supervised CNNs strongest on most considered tasks and greater ViT sensitivity to data and scale. assertions.source_quote: ViTs and CNNs are not interchangeable feature extractors even at similar accuracy. CKA analyses find more uniform, grid-like representations across ViT layers, clearer stage separation in ResNets, and link the ViT pattern to early global aggregation and strong residual propagation. Behavioral comparisons also show that similar ImageNet accuracy and compute can coexist with different mistakes, calibration, transferability, and invariances. Thus, no universal winner is supported. Pyramid, hybrid, or adapted Transformers may improve dense prediction or efficiency, but only under their specific architectures, pretraining, heads, datasets, and hardware conditions. assertions.source_quote: This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with convolutional neural-network backbones, using the organizing choice of backbone role rather than treating every later hybrid as a new version of ViT. The central question is not simply whether attention can replace convolution in classification: it is how a patch-based, globally attentive feature extractor compares with CNN feature extractors when both are used as backbones for recognition and downstream vision systems. CNN backbones such as ResNets and ResNeXts became the standard reusable feature extractors after large-scale ImageNet training, using local shared kernels whose receptive fields grow with depth and whose hierarchical feature maps fit detectors and segmenters. ViT instead entered vision as a convolution-free sequence model that splits an image into fixed patch tokens and applies standard Transformer self-attention across them; later work emphasizes that this plain design is distinct from vision-specific hierarchical Transformers and adapted CNN–Transformer backbones. assertions.source_quote: The scope therefore separates three levels of evidence. First, the original ViT should be understood as a classification-oriented, single-scale token backbone whose strongest early results depended on large-scale pretraining. Second, conventional CNN backbones should be assessed as hierarchical, locally connected feature extractors that were already integrated into dense-prediction pipelines. Third, later models such as PVT, CvT, LeViT, HVT, ConTNet, and ViT-CoMer respond to particular ViT limitations—resolution, hierarchy, local context, efficiency, optimization, or reuse of pretrained weights—but their results should not be read as direct measurements of the original ViT unless the training data, model size, task, decoder, and hardware conditions are matched. assertions.source_quote: Accordingly, the remainder of this review is grouped by mechanism and evidence: classification criteria, the original ViT and CNN mechanisms, matched or partially matched experimental results, and concrete trade-offs. Dense-prediction evidence is especially important because a backbone must supply spatially localized, often multi-scale features, not only an image-level class prediction. For example, PVT was explicitly motivated by ViT's low-resolution outputs and high computational and memory cost for dense tasks; under a comparable parameter count, RetinaNet with PVT-Small reached 40.4 AP on COCO val2017 versus 36.3 AP with ResNet-50. That result demonstrates a later pyramid Transformer's downstream advantage in that setup, but it does not establish that the original, unmodified ViT would outperform ResNet-50 under the same detector and training conditions. assertions.source_quote: For this review, the taxonomy is organized by backbone role: what spatial representation a feature extractor exposes, how tokens or feature maps change through depth, and whether the architecture can be inserted directly into classification and dense-prediction pipelines. assertions.source_quote: The first classification axis is output scale and spatial resolution. CNN backbones such as ResNet and ResNeXt provide stage-wise multi-scale feature maps that detectors and segmenters can consume through feature pyramids or decoder heads. The plain ViT paradigm is described as single-scale: it can exploit strong open-source ViT pretraining, but its limited scale diversity is insufficient for many dense-prediction requirements. Vision-specific pyramid Transformers such as PVT address this by redesigning the network into a progressive shrinking pyramid with spatial-reduction attention, whereas adapted backbones such as ViT-CoMer keep the plain ViT branch and add convolutional multi-scale features. These are distinct solutions to the same interface problem: a backbone used for detection or segmentation must provide localized, multi-resolution features, while an image classifier may only need a global representation. Vision-specific pyramid Transformers such as PVT address this by redesigning the network into a progressive shrinking pyramid with spatial-reduction attention, whereas adapted backbones such as ViT-CoMer keep the plain ViT branch and add convolutional multi-scale features. These are distinct solutions to the same interface problem: a backbone used for detection or segmentation must provide localized, multi-resolution features, while an image classifier may only need a global representation. assertions.source_quote: The second axis is locality versus global context. Convolution builds local receptive fields, translation-equivariant weight sharing, and spatial subsampling into its basic operation; stacked layers can eventually cover a large image region, but early layers do not attend globally in the ViT sense. ViT self-attention lets token positions interact dynamically over the full patch sequence, which representation analyses link to early aggregation of global information. CvT illustrates a hybrid position in this dimension: convolutional token embeddings and depth-wise-separable convolutional projections add overlapping local context, hierarchy, and subsampling while retaining Transformer attention. Thus, “CNN,” “plain ViT,” and “hybrid” should be separated by mechanism rather than treated as a simple accuracy label. assertions.source_quote: The third axis is positional encoding and input-resolution behavior. Standard ViT patch tokens need positional information because self-attention itself is permutation invariant; the original design therefore adds positional embeddings to patch embeddings. CvT reports that its convolutional design can remove positional embedding without performance degradation, which it presents as simplifying transfer to higher-resolution vision tasks. HVT instead progressively pools tokens to shorten the sequence, explicitly analogizing token downsampling to CNN feature-map downsampling. These criteria matter because changing resolution, token length, or position handling can affect both compute and compatibility with downstream heads; they are not merely implementation details. assertions.source_quote: The fourth axis is training dependence and optimization regime. Early ViT results showed that a pure Transformer could match or exceed strong CNNs in image classification when trained on sufficiently large data such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M; later work also notes that ViT-style models can be sensitive to learning rate, epochs, optimizer, augmentation, regularization, pretraining-data scale, and model size. CNN backbones established a different operating point as reusable, supervised ImageNet feature extractors, while later data-efficient and distilled Transformers reduced some of ViT's data requirements. Consequently, architecture family should not be conflated with pretraining recipe: a ViT trained on JFT, a CNN trained on ImageNet-1k, and a self-supervised backbone are not interchangeable observations even if their ImageNet top-1 scores are close. assertions.source_quote: The final axis separates task objective from efficiency objective. Classification asks for an image-level prediction; dense prediction asks for pixel-, box-, or mask-level outputs and therefore stresses resolution, localization, and multi-scale features. Efficiency-oriented designs form another related but different objective: LeViT reuses CNN principles such as decreasing activation-map resolutions and adds attention bias to optimize the speed–accuracy tradeoff for fast image classification, while HVT pools tokens to reduce sequence cost. Edge-splitting or model-pruning systems address deployment latency after a model exists and should not be confused with backbone taxonomy. Likewise, a formal unified view can interpret vision Transformers as CNNs with dynamic convolutions, but that analytical equivalence is a design-space perspective; it does not erase the practical differences in tokenization, feature hierarchy, pretraining, and downstream interfaces that govern the original ViT–CNN comparison. assertions.source_quote: The original ViT mechanism is deliberately close to a text Transformer: an image is divided into fixed-size, non-overlapping patches, each patch is linearly embedded, positional embeddings are added, and the resulting sequence is processed by repeated standard Transformer encoder blocks containing multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers. Its contribution was to show that a pure, convolution-free attention model could attain state-of-the-art image-classification performance against ResNets and EfficientNets when pretraining was large enough, specifically in regimes such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M. The applicability boundary is therefore central: the original architecture was primarily a global, single-scale image classifier rather than a ready-made feature pyramid for detectors and segmenters. Its evidence supports large-scale classification and transfer, not by itself a claim that the same token interface is efficient or optimal for high-resolution dense prediction. assertions.source_quote: Inside ViT, self-attention computes interactions among patch tokens rather than applying a fixed local kernel. This gives every token a path to information from the entire image at each attention layer, but the cost of full attention grows with the square of token count; high-resolution images therefore create substantially larger attention matrices and memory use. Representation analyses identify two consequences of this design. First, self-attention enables early aggregation of global information. Second, ViT residual connections strongly propagate lower-layer features into higher layers. These mechanisms help explain why ViT layers exhibit a more uniform representation structure than ResNet layers, but they do not imply that ViT automatically supplies the stage-wise spatial hierarchy used by common dense-prediction heads. assertions.source_quote: Conventional CNN backbones use a different inductive mechanism. A convolution kernel is applied locally with shared weights across spatial positions; stacked convolutional blocks expand the effective receptive field as network depth increases, while pooling or strided operations reduce spatial resolution and increase channel capacity. ResNet's skip connections made very deep convolutional networks practical, and ResNet/ResNeXt-style models became established reusable backbones because their stage outputs provide hierarchical feature maps for classification, detection, and segmentation. PVT's characterization of CNN backbones captures the key contrast: their local receptive fields increase with depth, whereas a Transformer can model global relations directly. The CNN contribution is therefore not merely convolution as an operator, but a mature hierarchy of local, translation-equivariant feature extraction with dense-prediction-compatible intermediate maps. assertions.source_quote: ResNet and similar CNNs are backbones in the operational sense: they expose multi-stage feature maps that can be connected to RetinaNet, Mask R-CNN, segmentation decoders, and other task-specific heads. This is why CNN backbones became common components across computer-vision systems rather than only standalone classifiers. Their applicability boundary is the reverse of plain ViT's: CNNs are naturally suited to local and hierarchical feature extraction, but ordinary convolutional layers do not perform ViT-style dynamic global token mixing at every block. A CNN can achieve a large aggregate receptive field, but that should not be described as identical to direct self-attention over all image patches. assertions.source_quote: The first major family of later responses is the pyramid Transformer. PVT retains a convolution-free Transformer backbone but changes the plain-ViT interface by constructing a progressive shrinking pyramid and using spatial-reduction attention. The pyramid learns multi-scale, high-resolution features while reducing the computation and memory burden of large feature maps; spatial-reduction attention shrinks the keys and values when processing high-resolution tokens. PVT's contribution was to make a pure Transformer usable as a drop-in backbone for representative dense-prediction pipelines such as RetinaNet and Mask R-CNN, and PVT plus DETR was presented as an entirely convolution-free detection pipeline. Its boundary is that it is a redesigned vision-specific backbone, not the original ViT model. Its convolutional Transformer block replaces the linear attention projections with depth-wise separable convolutional projections, adding local spatial context and allowing strided key/value subsampling for efficiency. Its convolutional token embedding uses overlapping strided convolutions on a two-dimensional token grid, capturing local context, reducing sequence length, and increasing feature dimension across stages. Its convolutional Transformer block replaces the linear attention projections with depth-wise separable convolutional projections, adding local spatial context and allowing strided key/value subsampling for efficiency. The claimed mechanism is a combination of CNN properties—local receptive fields, shared weights, and spatial subsampling—with Transformer properties—dynamic attention, global context fusion, and generalization. CvT's applicability is as a hierarchical hybrid classifier and transfer model; it is neither a plain ViT nor a conventional all-convolutional ResNet. assertions.source_quote: LeViT represents an efficiency-oriented hybrid rather than a direct dense-prediction backbone. It reintroduces convolutional-network principles into a vision Transformer, especially activation maps with decreasing resolution, and introduces attention bias as a way to integrate positional information. Its stated goal is fast inference image classification, with efficiency measured across hardware platforms rather than reduced to a single accuracy number. LeViT's contribution is a better speed–accuracy operating point in a high-speed classification regime; the abstract reports that at about 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy it is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. That evidence supports fast classification under the paper's hardware and evaluation settings, but it does not make LeViT a direct comparison of original ViT and ResNet for detection or segmentation. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:e4e92da5f487]

assertions.source_quote: HVT addresses another plain-ViT efficiency limitation: maintaining a full-length patch sequence throughout inference is redundant and lacks hierarchical representation. It progressively pools visual tokens to shrink sequence length, explicitly drawing an analogy to downsampling CNN feature maps. This permits increases in depth, width, input resolution, or patch-size-related capacity without paying the same full-sequence attention cost, and the paper reports that average-pooled visual tokens contain more discriminative information than a single class token in its empirical setting. HVT is therefore a hierarchical-token classification model. Its mechanism overlaps with CNN downsampling principles, but its results should be interpreted as evidence for token pooling in image classification, not as proof that CNNs and ViTs have equivalent representations. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

This permits increases in depth, width, input resolution, or patch-size-related capacity without paying the same full-sequence attention cost, and the paper reports that average-pooled visual tokens contain more discriminative information than a single class token in its empirical setting. HVT is therefore a hierarchical-token classification model. Its mechanism overlaps with CNN downsampling principles, but its results should be interpreted as evidence for token pooling in image classification, not as proof that CNNs and ViTs have equivalent representations. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

assertions.source_quote: ConTNet combines standard Transformer encoders with spatial convolution in a block-level hybrid design. A ConT block contains patch-wise standard Transformer encoder layers followed by a convolution layer; the Transformer models context within patches while the convolution processes the spatial grid. The authors position the design against two limitations: convolutional networks can lack sufficiently large receptive fields for downstream tasks, while vision Transformers can require special training settings or very large pretraining datasets. They claim ConTNet is easier to optimize than trendy visual Transformers and provides strong recognition and transfer behavior. Its evidence belongs to the conv–Transformer pattern category: it deliberately enlarges receptive fields through attention while retaining convolution, rather than isolating the original ViT mechanism. [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:3:aa366e49ea30:claim:164300ccc5ed] [E:arxiv:2104.13497:section:abstract:1:c29ac30f035c:claim:1a36e3385ae6]

assertions.source_quote: ViT-CoMer represents the adapted-backbone position: it preserves a plain ViT module so that advanced open-source ViT pretrained weights can be loaded, while adding convolutional multi-scale features rather than redesigning the entire Transformer. Its multi-receptive field feature pyramid supplies local and scale-diverse information that plain ViT lacks, and its CNN–Transformer bidirectional fusion interaction module fuses hierarchical convolutional features with Transformer features. The paper motivates this by two specific plain-ViT weaknesses in dense prediction: insufficient interaction within patches and limited feature-scale diversity. ViT-CoMer is therefore evidence that convolutional branches can compensate for plain ViT's dense-prediction interface while retaining access to ViT pretraining; it is not an unmodified ViT result. assertions.source_quote: ViT-CoMer represents the adapted-backbone position: it preserves a plain ViT module so that advanced open-source ViT pretrained weights can be loaded, while adding convolutional multi-scale features rather than redesigning the entire Transformer. Its multi-receptive field feature pyramid supplies local and scale-diverse information that plain ViT lacks, and its CNN–Transformer bidirectional fusion interaction module fuses hierarchical convolutional features with Transformer features. The paper motivates this by two specific plain-ViT weaknesses in dense prediction: insufficient interaction within patches and limited feature-scale diversity. ViT-CoMer is therefore evidence that convolutional branches can compensate for plain ViT's dense-prediction interface while retaining access to ViT pretraining; it is not an unmodified ViT result. assertions.source_quote: The distinction between plain, vision-specific, and adapted backbones is the paper's own paradigm and is useful for interpreting later evidence. A plain backbone can directly use advanced pretrained ViT weights but has limited scale diversity; a vision-specific backbone such as a pyramid Transformer builds multi-scale features into the network but may require structural changes and large-scale retraining; an adapted backbone keeps the original ViT and adds branches that can fuse CNN and Transformer features. ViT-CoMer initializes its ViT module from open-source pretrained weights while randomly initializing the added components. This trade-off between architectural fit and reuse of pretraining is one of the clearest practical differences between replacing a CNN backbone with plain ViT and using a modified Transformer backbone. assertions.source_quote: A separate line of work analyzes rather than hybridizes the two architectures. Raghu et al. use centered kernel alignment to compare internal representations and find that ViTs have a much more uniform, grid-like similarity structure, while ResNets divide more clearly into lower and higher stages. Cross-model CKA suggests that many lower ResNet layers resemble only the lowest quarter of ViT layers, the upper half of ResNet roughly corresponds to the next third of ViT layers, and the final third of ViT layers has little similar ResNet counterpart in their analysis. Through ablations, they attribute important differences to self-attention's early global aggregation and to residual connections that preserve lower-layer information. This supports a mechanism-level distinction even when both model families produce similar ImageNet predictions. assertions.source_quote: Broader benchmarking reinforces that architecture choice interacts with pretraining and evaluation target. Battle of the Backbones evaluates a diverse suite of pretrained backbones over classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization, and other tasks using more than 1,500 training runs. Its summary reports that supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-supervised SwinV2-Base, and CLIP ViT-Base are top performers at base scale, while supervised convolutional networks outperform Transformers on most tasks among the models considered. It also reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. These findings concern a modern backbone suite and multiple pretraining algorithms; they should not be reduced to a universal statement that every CNN beats every ViT, nor treated as a controlled test of only the original ViT and ResNet. assertions.source_quote: Finally, the unified dynamic-convolution interpretation offers a design-space bridge rather than a practical merger of architectures. It views vision Transformers as CNNs with dynamic convolutions, allowing Transformer and dynamic ConvNet choices to be compared side by side and transferred between design spaces. Its empirical examples include replacing softmax in Swin-Tiny attention with LayerNorm and ReLU, which the paper reports raises ImageNet top-1 accuracy from 81.13% to 81.56% without added compute, and constructing a depth-wise vision Transformer inspired by depth-wise convolution. This perspective is useful for mechanism analysis and network design, but it does not remove the empirical differences in tokenization, hierarchy, pretraining sensitivity, positional treatment, and dense-prediction interfaces established by the original ViT–CNN comparison. assertions.source_quote: The experimental comparison should be read by matched task and training regime rather than as one universal ViT-versus-CNN ranking. The original ViT evidence is strongest for image classification under large-scale pretraining: it decomposes images into non-overlapping patch tokens and applies standard Transformer blocks, and the cited literature describes it as the first pure Transformer to attain state-of-the-art classification against models such as ResNets and EfficientNets when trained on sufficiently large data such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M. That result is not directly comparable to a ResNet trained only on ImageNet-1k, because architecture, pretraining corpus, regularization, and model scale all change at once. A separate ImageNet-1k-from-scratch transformer literature therefore addresses a different question: whether modified or better regularized Transformers can become competitive without the original ViT's large-data regime. assertions.source_quote: Hybrid classification results likewise show that introducing convolution can improve the ViT operating point, but the reported numbers belong to the hybrid model. CvT uses hierarchical convolutional token embeddings and convolutional projections, and its paper reports state-of-the-art performance over other Vision Transformers and ResNets on ImageNet-1k with fewer parameters and lower FLOPs; after ImageNet-22k pretraining, CvT-W24 reached 87.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k validation. The paper also reports that positional encoding could be removed in CvT without degradation. Because CvT changes tokenization, hierarchy, projections, and positional treatment, these findings demonstrate a hybrid architecture's performance and efficiency under its training settings; they cannot be interpreted as the original ViT beating ResNet at identical FLOPs or as a generic CNN result. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency comparisons require the hardware, metric, and accuracy target to be kept together. LeViT was explicitly designed for fast inference image classification and combines decreasing-resolution activation maps with attention bias. At approximately 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy, the paper reports that LeViT is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. This supports a speed–accuracy advantage for LeViT over that EfficientNet baseline on the evaluated CPU regime; it does not imply lower FLOPs alone, lower GPU latency, or better dense-prediction performance. HVT supplies a separate classification-efficiency result: progressive token pooling shortens the patch sequence, and with comparable FLOPs the paper reports that HVT outperforms competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100. Those baselines and LeViT's CPU timing are not matched to one another, so the two studies should not be merged into a single efficiency ranking. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:e4e92da5f487] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:1b6019cff7cb]

assertions.source_quote: Representation experiments reveal differences that ImageNet accuracy alone does not capture. Using centered kernel alignment, Raghu et al. found that ViTs have a much more uniform, grid-like internal similarity structure, while ResNets separate more clearly into lower and higher stages; lower and higher ViT layers were also more similar to one another than lower and higher ResNet layers. Their cross-model analysis found that many lower ResNet layers corresponded roughly to only the lowest quarter of ViT layers, the upper half of ResNet to approximately the next third of ViT layers, and the final third of ViT layers had little similar ResNet counterpart. Ablations in that study linked the ViT pattern to early global aggregation through self-attention and strong propagation of lower-layer features through residual connections. These are mechanistic measurements on analyzed classification models, not accuracy or latency rankings. assertions.source_quote: Large modern backbone benchmarks broaden the empirical picture but mix architectures and pretraining protocols. Battle of the Backbones reports more than 1,500 training runs across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization, and other tasks; among its considered models, supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-supervised SwinV2-Base, and CLIP ViT-Base were top base-scale performers, while supervised convolutional networks performed best on most tasks. The same summary reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count, and that apples-to-apples comparisons at similar pretraining-data scale make self-supervised backbones highly competitive. These findings should not be converted into a direct ResNet-beats-original-ViT verdict because the suite includes ConvNeXt, SwinV2, CLIP, MAE, MoCo, DINO, and other modern systems with different datasets and learning objectives. assertions.source_quote: Beyond-Backbones further limits the usefulness of a single ImageNet ranking. In a controlled comparative analysis of ConvNet and Vision Transformer architectures across supervised and CLIP training paradigms, models selected for similar ImageNet accuracy and compute still differed in the types of mistakes they made, output calibration, transferability, and feature invariance. Therefore, even when top-1 accuracy and nominal compute are matched, the experimental decision between a ViT-like and convolutional backbone can depend on calibration, robustness, transfer target, and the desired invariances. The selected evidence supports a conditional conclusion: original ViT is a strong large-data global classifier but is not naturally a CNN-style multi-scale dense-prediction backbone; CNN backbones offer mature hierarchical maps and a strong broad-task baseline; and pyramid, hybrid, or adapted Transformers can close or reverse particular downstream gaps only under their stated architectures, pretraining, heads, datasets, and hardware settings. assertions.source_quote: The first open problem is that the original ViT's strongest classification evidence does not transfer automatically to the backbone role needed for dense prediction. Plain ViT preserves patch locations and can reason globally, but its native single-scale token sequence lacks the stage-wise, multi-resolution feature interface that detectors and segmenters expect from CNN backbones. PVT explicitly identifies low-resolution outputs, high computational cost, and high memory cost as barriers to porting ViT to pixel-level tasks, while ViT-CoMer separately identifies insufficient inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity. The implication is that downstream users cannot infer detection or segmentation suitability from ImageNet performance alone; they must evaluate spatial resolution, scale diversity, decoder compatibility, token count, and memory together. assertions.explanation: ViT-CoMer explicitly states ViT does not perform well in dense prediction due to lack of inner-patch information interaction.

assertions.source_quote: The first open problem is that the original ViT's strongest classification evidence does not transfer automatically to the backbone role needed for dense prediction. Plain ViT preserves patch locations and can reason globally, but its native single-scale token sequence lacks the stage-wise, multi-resolution feature interface that detectors and segmenters expect from CNN backbones. PVT explicitly identifies low-resolution outputs, high computational cost, and high memory cost as barriers to porting ViT to pixel-level tasks, while ViT-CoMer separately identifies insufficient inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity. The implication is that downstream users cannot infer detection or segmentation suitability from ImageNet performance alone; they must evaluate spatial resolution, scale diversity, decoder compatibility, token count, and memory together. assertions.source_quote: A second, closely related problem is the quadratic cost of full self-attention as image resolution grows. A conventional CNN controls dense-feature cost through strided convolution and stage-wise downsampling, whereas maintaining a full-length ViT patch sequence creates larger attention maps and can make high-resolution inference expensive. PVT responds with a progressive shrinking pyramid and spatial-reduction attention, and HVT responds by progressively pooling tokens. These are credible mitigations, but they also change the architecture and its outputs; they do not make the original plain ViT free of the resolution–memory trade-off. FLOP reductions likewise should not be treated as latency reductions unless the relevant hardware and runtime are measured. assertions.source_quote: The third problem is pretraining dependence. The original pure-Transformer recipe became competitive with strong CNN classifiers when large datasets such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M were available, while ConTNet notes that vision Transformers can be sensitive to learning rate, training epochs, optimizer, augmentation, and other settings. Battle of the Backbones similarly reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and to parameter count. This makes model comparisons conditional: a ViT pretrained on a huge corpus, a CNN supervised on ImageNet-1k, and a self-supervised backbone answer different empirical questions. The practical limitation is that reproducing ViT's best classification regime may require data, compute, and regularization unavailable for a specialized vision task. assertions.source_quote: Fourth, architectural modification often creates a pretraining-reuse trade-off. Vision-specific pyramid Transformers can build the hierarchical features needed for dense prediction, but changing the plain ViT structure can prevent direct reuse of existing powerful ViT checkpoints and may require large-scale retraining. ViT-CoMer's adapted design illustrates the alternative: keep the original ViT module so open-source pretrained weights can be loaded, add convolutional multi-scale branches, and randomly initialize the added components. This improves task fit but introduces new modules, fusion complexity, and a training burden for the CNN branch. The unresolved practical issue is therefore not only how to obtain multi-scale features, but whether doing so preserves the value of already learned ViT representations. assertions.source_quote: Sixth, the internal-representation evidence shows that similar predictions do not imply similar visual processing. assertions.source_quote: Seventh, locality and global context remain a genuine trade-off rather than a solved choice. Ordinary CNN layers impose local receptive fields, shared weights, and spatial subsampling, which help encode local visual structure efficiently but require depth or specialized modules to model very long-range relations. ViT attention directly mixes distant patch tokens, but the original design lacks convolution's built-in local processing and progressive hierarchy. Hybrid models such as CvT and ConTNet show that convolutional tokenization, convolutional projections, or block-level convolution can add local context, but they also make it impossible to attribute a result purely to either self-attention or convolution. The open problem is how to obtain local bias and adaptive global mixing without paying the full cost, retraining cost, or confounding both mechanisms in evaluation. assertions.source_quote: Eighth, variable-resolution deployment remains difficult because positional treatment and token density interact. The original ViT relies on positional embeddings in a permutation-invariant attention architecture, whereas CvT reports that its convolutional projections and embeddings allow positional encoding to be removed without degradation, simplifying higher-resolution use. That finding is design-specific and should not be generalized to plain ViT. High-resolution multimodal and edge systems also face excessive visual tokens, quadratic complexity, latency, and memory pressure; proposed responses include hierarchical ConvNeXt encoders, token compression, model splitting, and class-wise pruning. These systems address deployment constraints after architecture choice and do not establish that the original ViT has a native resolution-robust solution. assertions.source_quote: Finally, the field lacks a clean universal ranking because benchmark suites mix architecture, pretraining objective, dataset scale, model size, task head, and hardware. Battle of the Backbones finds supervised convolutional networks strongest on most tasks among the models it considered, yet also reports top performance for specific supervised SwinV2 and CLIP ViT variants and competitive self-supervised models in apples-to-apples dataset-scale comparisons. PVT and ViT-CoMer show strong dense-prediction results for redesigned or adapted Transformers, while LeViT and HVT address particular efficiency regimes. These findings are complementary, not interchangeable: the original ViT, ResNet-like CNNs, hybrid models, and modern pretrained backbones must be compared under matched tasks and settings before one can claim general superiority. assertions.source_quote: Strong downstream Transformer results should be assigned to the modified architecture and recipe. PVT's 40.4 versus 36.3 AP RetinaNet advantage over ResNet-50 reflects a pyramid Transformer with spatial-reduction attention, and ViT-CoMer's reported 64.3% COCO AP and 62.1% ADE20K mIoU reflect an adapted ViT with convolutional multi-scale branches and fusion.
